title: Cap. VIII Resp.: negative reprobation is not from punitive justice; permission precedes foresight of final bad use
pass_a_gloss: Negative reprobation, which says nothing other than the eternal purpose of God concerning not giving to certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened, and by whose benefit they themselves would be infallibly directed unto eternal life, does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from the will of damning, but from that reason of Divine providence by which God judged it to agree with his wisdom that he should permit certain ones by their own vice to fall short of the end of beatitude. But this will of God being posited, God foresights the future sins of the reprobate, and their final remaining in sins; and at the same time understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from the punishment of sins. God therefore intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobated, on account of the sins in which they are foresighted as about to finish life; but this intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as also the final state itself of the sinner in his sins. We can indeed say, and truly, that there always was in God a will of punishing sins, if they should come to be: but an absolute and express will of punishing, and terminated unto this or that singular person, we cannot place in God, unless the permission of God that they should come to be be presupposed, and that this person destined unto punishment should finally remain under the guilt of the same. But this permission, which contains the act of negative reprobation, is prior to the absolute foresight of the evil use of free will lasting unto the end of life in this or that singular person, and therefore cannot depend from that as from a cause. Wrongly therefore are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or of damning deduced from the same causes.
pass_b_english: Negative reprobation — nothing but God's eternal purpose not to give certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened and by which they would be infallibly directed to eternal life — does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from a will to damn, but from that reason of providence by which God judged it agreeable to his wisdom to permit some, by their own vice, to fall short of beatitude's end. That will posited, God foresights the reprobate's future sins and final remaining in them, and understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from punishing those sins. So he intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobate for the sins in which they are foresighted as finishing life — but that intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as did the sinner's final state in his sins. We may truly say there was always in God a will to punish sins if they should come to be; but an absolute express will to punish, terminated on this or that particular person, we cannot place in God unless his permission that they come to be is presupposed, and that this person destined to punishment finally remain under their guilt. That permission — which contains the act of negative reprobation — is prior to absolute foresight of evil use of free will lasting to life's end in this or that person, and so cannot depend on that foresight as cause. Wrongly, then, are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or damning drawn from the same causes.
source_text: Reprobatio negativa, quae nihil aliud dicit quam aeternum Dei propositum de non-dando quibusdam singularem gratiam qua corda illorum emollirentur, cujusque beneficio ipsi ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter dirigerentur, non procedit ex justitia punitiva, neque ex voluntate damnandi, sed ex illa Divinae providentiae ratione, qua Deus judicavit sapientiae suae convenire, ut permitteret quosdam suo vitio a fine beatitudinis deficere. Posita autem hac Dei voluntate, praevidet Deus futura reproborum peccata, et finalem eorundem permansionem in peccatis; atque simul intelligit gloriae suae manifestationem ex punitione peccatorum orituram. Intendit itaque Deus justitiam punitivam exercere circa reprobates, propter peccata in quibus praevidentur vitam finitori; sed haec intentio et praevisio secuta est reprobationis praedictae actum, sicuti et ipse finalis status peccatoris in peccatis suis. Dicere quidem possumus, et vere, semper fuisse in Deo voluntatem puniendi peccata, si fierent: sed absolutam et expressam voluntatem puniendi, ac terminatam ad hanc aut illam singularem personam, non possumus in Deo ponere, nisi praesupposita Dei permissione ut fierent, utque haec persona punitioni destinata sub reatu eorundem finaliter permaneret. Haec autem permissio, quae reprobationis negativae actum continet, prior est absoluta praescientia mali usus liberi arbitrii ad finem vitae usque perdurantis in hac aut illa persona singulari, ac proinde non potest ex illa tanquam ex causa dependere. Perperam ergo reprobandi ac vindicandi sive damnandi decreta ex iisdem causis deducuntur.
